name: Nara
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Thompson, David E. 1976, 'Nera', in M. L. Bender (ed.), The Non-Semitic Languages of Ethiopia, 484-494 (phonological sketch; cited on Wikipedia); not online.

new_statements.quote: Nara is a tone language. The tone-bearing unit is the mora and, in addition to vowels, post-vocalic glides and sonorant consonants also carry tone. Tones are associated independently with each mora of a long vowel. [...] Thompson (1976: 484) makes certain tentative comments about stress in Nara, but we find no convincing evidence for this additional prosodic feature, and the examples adduced by Thompson seem to lend themselves to a simpler analysis in terms of length (gemination) of the following consonant.
new_statements.citation: Abushush Dawd & Richard J. Hayward. 2002. Nara. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 32(2): 249-255. DOI 10.1017/S0025100302001068
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nara is a two-tone (H/L) mora-tone language; the JIPA authors explicitly find no evidence for word stress as a separate prosodic feature and reanalyse Thompson's (1976: 484) 'stress on any syllable, contrastive' examples ('iŋŋa vs iŋ'ŋa) as gemination of the following consonant. The one older source with an accent rule, Reinisch 1874 (pp. 19-20, from Munzinger's acute marks), restricts the 'accent' to one of the last three syllables of the word, never retracting beyond the antepenult, staying on the stem syllable under plural suffixation (suffix never accented), with penult accent in -ado/-edo abstract nouns and person-dependent accent in verb paradigms (p. 61) - a lexical/morphological accent within a three-syllable window that most plausibly records the high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Thompson 1976 p. 484 claims contrastive stress on any syllable, with 'CVCV -> 'CVCCV gemination after a stressed first syllable; Abushush & Hayward 2002 reject this as stress. Reinisch 1874 notes his manuscript inconsistently gives dlédo 'gang' beside the penult rule for -ado/-edo nouns.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (moras; citation forms), with a phonological-phrase constraint against two non-contiguous H tones that deletes an expected H on the syntactic head; the stress denial concerns the word. Speaker described: Higir dialect (higi1240).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Abushush & Hayward 2002) describes the speech of one 31-year-old male speaker of the Higir dialect (higi1240, Eastern Nara), the basis of the emerging standard; Hayward 2000 is likewise Higir. Thompson 1976 'Nera' and Reinisch 1874 'Barea' (Munzinger's 1860s manuscript material) are the same language under older names, dialect unspecified.

sources.citation: Abushush Dawd & Richard J. Hayward. 2002. Nara. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 32(2): 249-255. DOI 10.1017/S0025100302001068
sources.quote: Nara is a tone language. The tone-bearing unit is the mora and, in addition to vowels, post-vocalic glides and sonorant consonants also carry tone. Tones are associated independently with each mora of a long vowel. [...] Thompson (1976: 484) makes certain tentative comments about stress in Nara, but we find no convincing evidence for this additional prosodic feature, and the examples adduced by Thompson seem to lend themselves to a simpler analysis in terms of length (gemination) of the following consonant.
sources.note: pp. 249-250 'Tone': Nara is a tone language (H/L on moras; contours = tone sequences; H dropped on phrase heads to avoid two non-contiguous Hs in a phonological phrase); p. 250: Thompson (1976: 484) makes tentative comments about stress, 'but we find no convincing evidence for this additional prosodic feature' - his examples are reanalysed as gemination of the following consonant. Speaker: Higir dialect.

sources.citation: Reinisch, Leo. 1874. Die Barea-Sprache: Grammatik, Text und Wörterbuch (nach den handschriftlichen Materialien von Werner Munzinger Pascha). Wien: Wilhelm Braumüller. (Google scan, archive.org item diebareasprache00reingoog)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online: WID Offsite Storage 2246.97; FIG HathiTrust (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Lautlehre pp. 19-20 (PDF pp. 56-57; page images saved): accent = Munzinger's acute; 'Der accent kann nur auf einer der drei lezten silben des wortes ruhen'; never retracts beyond the antepenult (adjective plurals antepenult); otherwise stays on the stem syllable in the plural (hágga pl. hággita); plural suffix never accented; abstract nouns in -ado/-edo accented on the penult. p. 61 (PDF p. 110): passive perfect accent on the penult in 1pl, antepenult in the other persons. No tone recognised.

sources.citation: Thompson, David E. 1976. Nera. In M. Lionel Bender (ed.), The Non-Semitic Languages of Ethiopia, 484-494. East Lansing: African Studies Center, Michigan State University. (Only p. 484 opened: Rosetta Project excerpt on archive.org, item rosettaproject_nrb_phon-1)
sources.note: p. 484 §2.2 Stress: 'Stress may come on any syllable and can cause change of meaning, e.g. 'iŋŋa "you (singular)", iŋ'ŋa "you (plural)". When the first of two CV syllables is stressed, the second C becomes doubled with short vowels: 'CVCV -> 'CVCCV.' §2.3 Tone: 'At least two significant tones occur: normal and high.' (page image verified:)
